title: Fruity hues
q: Both a fruit and a colour
rule: Botanical fruits count even when cooks treat them as vegetables, and the colour must be a standard colour name.

traps.Violet: A colour, but not a fruit.
traps.Mustard: A colour, but not a fruit.

fact: Cranberries float when ripe because they hold air pockets, which is why growers flood the bogs to harvest them.

title: Wild wheels
q: An animal that's also a car
rule: Model or brand names sold in some markets count, but trim levels and engine names don't.

traps.Lion: Peugeot uses a lion as its badge, but that is a logo rather than a model name.

fact: The Fiat Panda was styled by Giorgetto Giugiaro, who also designed the first Volkswagen Golf.

title: Eponymous eats
q: A food or drink named after a real person
rule: Dishes and drinks widely said to be named after a real person count, even where the story is disputed.

traps.Waldorf Salad: Named after a hotel, not a person.
traps.Chicken Kiev: Named after a city, not a person.

fact: The sandwich is named after John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, who reportedly asked for meat between bread so he could keep gambling.

title: Same both ways
q: A word that reads the same backwards
rule: Single ordinary English words only, so names, abbreviations and phrases don't count.

traps.Anna: A palindrome, but it is a first name rather than an everyday word.
traps.Stats: A palindrome, but it is an abbreviation rather than an everyday word.

fact: Pip is a palindrome, and it is also the name of the narrator in Dickens's Great Expectations.

title: Feathered verbs
q: A bird that's also an everyday verb
rule: Any bird whose name is also an everyday verb counts, including informal and sports senses, but nouns and adjectives don't.

traps.Owl: A bird, but it is not used as an everyday verb.
traps.Wren: A bird, but it is not used as an everyday verb.

fact: The little stint is one of the smallest shorebirds in the world, and 'stint' is also a verb meaning to be sparing.

title: Urban namesakes
q: A city that's also a first name
rule: Only cities and towns count, and the word must be a common first name; states and countries with the same name don't.

traps.Brighton: A city, but it is not used as a first name.
traps.Julia: A first name, but it is not a city.

fact: Adelaide was named after Queen Adelaide, the wife of King William IV.

title: Hero endings
q: A character whose name ends in -man
rule: Fictional characters from films, comics, games, TV and books count, but real people with these names don't.

traps.Hulk: A comic hero, but his name doesn't end this way.
traps.Frosty: A snowman, but his name isn't Snowman.

fact: Pac-Man was originally released in Japan as Puck Man, and the name was changed for the Western release.

title: Red-letter dates
rule: Named calendar dates count, while nights and eves such as Bonfire Night and Burns Night don't.

traps.Bonfire Night: A named night rather than a date, so the rule excludes it.
traps.Burns Night: A named night rather than a date, so the rule excludes it.
traps.Halloween: It's All Hallows' Eve, and eves don't count here.

fact: Groundhog Day began as a US tradition in 1887, when a Pennsylvania town first asked a groundhog about the weather.

title: Suffix tour
q: A country whose name ends in -land or -stan
rule: Sovereign states and the UK's home nations count, while territories and US states with the same endings don't.

traps.Greenland: Ends in -land, but it is a Danish territory, so the rule excludes it.
traps.Maryland: Ends in -land, but it is a US state, not a country.
traps.Kurdistan: A region, not a sovereign state.

fact: Pakistan was coined in 1933 as an acronym for its regions, and '-stan' is a Persian word meaning land.

title: Fab name drop
q: A Beatles song with a person's name in its title
rule: Real or fictional people count when a first or full name is in the title, but songs named after places like Penny Lane don't.

head: Hey Jude
Michelle
Eleanor Rigby
Dear Prudence
Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds
body: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band

Ballad of John and Yoko: The Ballad of John and Yoko

traps.Penny Lane: A Beatles song, but its title names a street rather than a person.

fact: Hey Jude was first titled 'Hey Jules', written as a song of encouragement for John Lennon's son Julian.

title: Light on your feet
q: A dance whose name is also an everyday word
rule: Only dances whose name is also an ordinary English word count, so proper names and purely foreign dance terms don't.

traps.Samba: A dance, but its name is not an everyday English word.
traps.Mambo: A dance, but its name is not an everyday English word.

fact: The cakewalk began as a 19th-century dance contest in the American South, with a cake as the prize.

title: Body language
q: A part of the body that's also a verb
rule: Any body part whose name is a standard dictionary verb counts, including informal ones, while adjectives and nouns don't.

traps.Ankle: A body part, but it is not used as an everyday verb.
traps.Hip: A body part, but it is not used as an everyday verb.

fact: The phrase 'knuckle down' comes from marbles, where players had to keep their knuckles on the ground while shooting.

title: Fishy words
q: A fish whose name is also an everyday word
rule: Only the plain species name counts, and the word must be an ordinary English word, so proper names and prepared fish dishes don't.

traps.Eel: A fish, but its name is not an everyday word on its own.
traps.Kipper: A smoked herring, not a fish name.

fact: The bleak is a small silvery freshwater fish, and it shares a name with the everyday adjective for something cheerless.

title: Colourful names
q: A colour that's also a first name
rule: Only colours that are also common given names count, and surnames or place names with the same spelling don't.

traps.Mauve: A colour, but it is not a common first name.
traps.Taupe: A colour, but it is not a first name.

fact: The colour heather is named after a purple flowering shrub, and the same word has long been a popular first name.
